items.title: Why infrastructure as code
items.context: IaC describes infrastructure in versioned files so changes are reviewed in pull requests, reproducible across environments and auditable. Declarative tools (Terraform, CloudFormation) describe the desired end state; the tool works out the steps.

questions.prompt: In a declarative tool like Terraform, you write:
choices: The desired end state; the tool computes the changes
Shell scripts executed on every server
questions.explanation: Terraform diffs desired state against current state to build a plan.

items.title: The core workflow
items.context: terraform init downloads providers and modules and configures the backend. terraform plan shows what would change. terraform apply makes the changes (after another confirmation unless you pass a saved plan). terraform fmt and validate keep code clean.

questions.prompt: Which command shows what will change without changing anything?
questions.explanation: Save it with -out=tfplan and apply that exact plan in CI.

items.title: State
items.context: The state file maps resources in your code to real infrastructure IDs. Teams store it in a remote backend (S3 with locking, Terraform Cloud, GCS…) so everyone shares it and two applies can't run at once. State can contain secrets, so encrypt it and restrict access.

questions.prompt: Why use a remote backend with state locking for a team?
choices: Everyone shares one state and two concurrent applies can't corrupt it
questions.explanation: Local state on laptops diverges and gets lost; locking prevents races.

questions.prompt: Should terraform.tfstate be committed to Git?
choices: No — it can hold secrets and is better in a locked remote backend
questions.explanation: Add it to .gitignore.

items.title: Providers, resources, data sources
items.context: Providers talk to an API (aws, azurerm, kubernetes). A resource block creates and manages an object. A data block only reads something that already exists (the latest AMI, an existing VPC) without managing it.

questions.prompt: You need the ID of a VPC created by another team, without managing it. Use:
questions.explanation: data "aws_vpc" "shared" { tags = { Name = "shared" } } reads it.

items.title: Variables, locals, outputs
items.context: Input variables parameterise a configuration or module, locals name intermediate expressions, and outputs expose values to the caller (a parent module, the CLI, or terraform_remote_state).

questions.prompt: How does a module hand its VPC ID back to the configuration that calls it?
questions.explanation: The caller reads it as module.network.vpc_id.

items.title: Modules
items.context: A module is a reusable directory of Terraform code with inputs and outputs. Pin module and provider versions (version = "~> 5.0") so an upstream release doesn't change your infrastructure unexpectedly.

questions.prompt: Why pin module versions?
choices: So upstream changes don't silently alter your next plan
questions.explanation: Upgrade deliberately, reading the plan.

items.title: Drift and import
items.context: Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches the code, usually after manual console changes; terraform plan reveals it. Existing, unmanaged resources can be brought under Terraform with terraform import or an import block (Terraform 1.5+).

questions.prompt: Someone created an S3 bucket by hand and you want Terraform to manage it. Use:
questions.explanation: Write the resource block, import the existing ID, then plan until it shows no changes.

items.title: count vs for_each
items.context: count creates copies addressed by index (aws_instance.web[0]); removing an item from the middle shifts later indexes, so Terraform plans to destroy and recreate them. for_each keys instances by map key or set value (aws_instance.web["api"]), so removing one only affects that one.

questions.prompt: You manage a list of 5 users with count and remove the 2nd one. The plan:
choices: Changes or recreates the users after it, because their indexes shift
questions.explanation: Use for_each = toset(var.users) for collections whose items change.

items.title: lifecycle
items.context: lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } builds the replacement before destroying the old resource (avoids downtime). prevent_destroy = true makes any plan that would destroy it fail. ignore_changes skips attributes changed outside Terraform.

questions.prompt: Which setting protects a production database from an accidental destroy?
questions.explanation: Apply then errors instead of deleting it.

items.title: Environments
items.context: Each environment (dev, staging, prod) needs its own state. Common approaches: separate directories or root modules per environment (often sharing modules), or Terraform workspaces. Separate backends and credentials for prod reduce the blast radius.

questions.prompt: What must never be shared between dev and prod?
questions.explanation: One shared state means a dev apply could change prod.

items.title: Variable files
items.context: Values for input variables come from terraform.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars (loaded automatically), -var-file=prod.tfvars, -var flags, or TF_VAR_name environment variables.

questions.prompt: Which file is loaded automatically without a flag?
questions.explanation: Use -var-file for environment-specific files.

items.title: Sensitive values
items.context: sensitive = true on a variable or output hides its value in plan and apply output, but it's still stored in plain text in the state file. Protect the state, or keep secrets out of Terraform and fetch them at run time.

questions.prompt: With sensitive = true, the database password is:
choices: Hidden in CLI output but still present in state
Sent to the provider in a hash only
questions.explanation: Encrypt the backend (e.g. S3 with KMS) and restrict who can read it.

items.title: depends_on
items.context: Terraform orders operations from references between resources. depends_on adds an explicit dependency when one isn't visible in the code, e.g. an app that needs an IAM policy attachment to exist first. Prefer real references when possible.

questions.prompt: When do you need depends_on?
choices: When a dependency exists but no attribute reference expresses it
questions.explanation: Overusing it serialises applies and hides design problems.

items.title: Refactoring without recreation
items.context: Renaming a resource or moving it into a module changes its address, so Terraform would plan to destroy the old one and create a new one. A moved { from = … to = … } block (or terraform state mv) tells Terraform it's the same object.

questions.prompt: You renamed aws_db_instance.main to aws_db_instance.primary and the plan wants to destroy the database. Fix:
choices: Add a moved block from the old address to the new one
questions.explanation: The plan then shows no change.

items.title: Provider lock file
items.context: .terraform.lock.hcl records the exact provider versions and checksums chosen by terraform init. Commit it, so CI and teammates use identical providers; upgrade deliberately with terraform init -upgrade.

questions.prompt: Should .terraform.lock.hcl be committed?
choices: Yes — it pins provider versions and checksums for everyone
questions.explanation: The .terraform/ directory itself stays ignored.

items.title: Sharing outputs between stacks
items.context: One configuration can read another's outputs with the terraform_remote_state data source (or through a parameter store such as SSM), e.g. an app stack reading the VPC ID from the network stack.

questions.prompt: The app stack needs the network stack's subnet IDs. A common approach:
choices: Copy and paste the IDs into the code
Merge both stacks into one state
Read them via terraform_remote_state (or a parameter store)
questions.explanation: Small, separate states reduce the blast radius of each apply.

items.title: Plan in pull requests
items.context: A common team flow: CI runs terraform plan on every pull request and posts the diff for review; after merge, the reviewed plan is applied (tools like Atlantis or Terraform Cloud automate this). Nobody applies from a laptop.

questions.prompt: Why post terraform plan output on pull requests?
choices: It removes the need for state
Reviewers see the real infrastructure changes before they happen
questions.explanation: Code diffs don't show that a change would replace a database; plans do.

items.title: Dynamic blocks
items.context: A dynamic block generates repeated nested blocks from a collection, e.g. one ingress { } block per entry in a list of ports inside an aws_security_group.

questions.prompt: To create one ingress rule block per port in var.ports inside a resource, use:
questions.explanation: Use it sparingly; too much dynamism makes code hard to read.

items.title: Terraform vs CloudFormation
items.context: CloudFormation is AWS-native and AWS-only, with state managed by AWS. Terraform (and its open-source fork OpenTofu) uses providers for many clouds and SaaS APIs with one language (HCL), but you manage the state.

questions.prompt: One tool to manage AWS, Cloudflare DNS and Datadog monitors together:
questions.explanation: That's the provider ecosystem's strength.
